This is also the condition of those who follow their desires: they take pleasure in them at first, and then pains follow in proportion to what they obtained from them. And those who refrain from them gain, by their loss, at first, and then pain is followed by pleasure and delight in proportion to what they refrained from and abandoned. So pain and pleasure are a necessity for every human being. But the difference between the small, transient, immediate and the great, enduring, deferred is vast. This is why the distinctive trait of reason is to consider consequences and final ends. Whoever thinks that he can free himself from pain such that it never touches him at all, his thought is the most false of falsehoods. For man is created exposed to pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow, delight and grief. This comes from two aspects: from his composition, nature and constitution, for he is composed of humors that are varied and opposed, whose balance is impossible or very difficult to achieve in every respect; rather, some of them must inevitably transgress against others and depart from the limit of balance, so pain arises. And from his fellow-human beings, for he is naturally social, unable to live alone, and cannot live except with them. He and they have pleasures and aims that are opposed and conflicting, and they cannot be combined; rather, when one of them is attained, others are lost. He wants them to agree with his aims and will, and they want the same from him. If he agrees with them, he suffers pain and hardship in proportion to what he has lost of his own will. If he does not agree with them, they harm him, torment him, and strive to nullify his aims, just as he did not agree with their aims. So he suffers pain and torment accordingly. He is therefore in pain, hardship and toil, whether he agrees with them or opposes them. This is especially so when their agreement is upon matters that he knows to be false beliefs, corrupt wills and deeds that harm him in their consequences. In agreeing with them there is the greatest pain, and in opposing them there is the arising of pain. So reason, religion, manliness and knowledge command him to bear the lesser of two pains, in order to be freed from the greater, and to prefer the transient of the two so as to be saved from the enduring and continuous one.

Whoever supports the criminal oppressors in their oppression, or the people of whims and innovations in their whims and innovations, or the people of immorality and desires in their immorality and desires, in order to be freed by supporting them from the pain of their harm, will suffer from agreeing with them, both immediately and in the future, many times more than what he fled from. It is God's custom with His creation that He punishes them for their faith and their support of them, even if he endures the pain of opposing them and keeping away from them. That endurance will bring him an immediate and future pleasure that exceeds the pleasure of agreement by manifold. It is God's custom with His creation that He raises him above them and humiliates them through him, in proportion to his patience, piety, trust in Him and sincerity. If the pain and punishment are of this kind, then in God and in seeking His good pleasure and following His messengers, it is more fitting and more beneficial than in pursuing people's pleasure, their approval and fulfilling their aims. Since the time of pain and punishment is long, his patience is long: his breaths are hours, his hours are days, his days are months and years. God, the Exalted, tested them in it by informing them that this trial is deferred and then will end. He set for its people a term for meeting Him, to console them with it, to comfort their souls, and to make its burdens light for them. He said: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming; and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

So when the servant contemplates the term of that trial and its ending, and the term of meeting Him, the Tester, the Exalted, and its affirmation, what he is in becomes easy for him and its burden becomes light. Then, since that cannot be achieved except through striving against the self, against Satan, and against his fellow human beings, and since the worker who knows that the fruit of his knowledge and his toil returns to him alone, without anyone else thanking him for it, makes his effort more complete and his striving more abundant, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever strives, he strives only for himself; surely God is Self-Sufficient above the worlds.﴾ Also, no one should imagine that the benefit of this striving, patience and endurance returns to God, the Exalted, for He is independent of the worlds. He did not command them with what He commanded out of any need for them, nor forbid them from what He forbade out of stinginess towards them. Rather, He commanded them with what returns benefit and welfare to them in their livelihood and their hereafter, and forbade them from what returns harm and ruin to them in their livelihood and their hereafter. So the fruit of this trial and testing is specific to them. His wisdom required that He establish this as a decreed cause to distinguish the wicked from the good, the miserable from the misguided, and who is fit for it from who is not fit. He said: ﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.﴾ So God, the Exalted, tested them by sending messengers to them with His commands and prohibitions and His choosing. Thus, by His messengers, their good was distinguished from their wicked, and their excellent from their inferior. Reward and punishment then fell upon a known matter that this trial and testing made manifest.

Then, since the one being tested must inevitably deviate from the path of patience and striving, due to the impulses of his nature, his desire, and his weakness in resisting what he was tested with, the Exalted promised that He would overlook that for him and expiate it, because when he was commanded and bound himself to obedience, His mercy required that He expiate his misdeeds and reward him with the best of his deeds. Then the Exalted mentioned the servant's trial with his parents, and what he was commanded regarding obeying them, and his patience in striving against them that he should not associate anything with Him. So he should be patient in this ordeal and tribulation and not obey them, but accompany them in this state with kindness, and turn away from them to follow the way of His messengers. In turning away from them and their way, and turning towards those who oppose them and towards His way, there is a test and trial with what it contains. Then the Exalted mentioned the condition of one who entered faith with weak resolve, little patience, and no steadfastness under the ordeal and trial. When he is harmed for God, as the custom of God is and as His wisdom requires in testing His friends through His enemies and giving them power over them with various kinds of hardship and harm, he does not endure that; he panics, flees from it, and from its causes, as one flees from the punishment of God. So He made the people's persecution of him for faith and obedience to His messengers like the punishment of God for whoever punishes him for associating partners with God and opposing His messengers. This indicates lack of insight, and that faith has not entered his heart nor has he tasted its sweetness, to the point that he equated God's punishment of him for faith in God and His messenger with God's punishment of whoever does not believe in Him and His messengers. This is the condition of one who worships God on an edge, whose foot has not been firmly planted in faith and the worship of God. He is among the tested and tormented, even if he escapes the people's punishment of him for faith. Then He mentioned the condition of this person at the time of the victory of the believers, that when they are granted victory he comes to them and says, "I was with you," while God knows what his heart conceals contrary to his words.

Then the Exalted mentioned the trial of Noah with his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and the trial of his people with obedience to him, so they denied him, and He tested them with the flood, then after that with the storm. Then He mentioned the trial of Abraham with his people, and how they rejected him, and He tested them with obeying and following him. Then He mentioned the trial of Lot with his people, and their trial with him, and what his affair and theirs came to. Then He mentioned the trial of Shu'ayb with his people, and their trial with him, and what their state and his came to. Then He mentioned what He tested 'Ad and Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh, Haman and their armies with, of faith in Him and worshipping Him alone, then the various punishments with which He tested them. Then He mentioned the trial of His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) with various kinds of disbelievers, from idolaters and People of the Book, and commanded him to argue with the People of the Book in the best manner. Then He commanded His servants who were tested by His enemies to migrate from their land to His vast land, to worship Him there. Then He alerted them, through the greater migration from the abode of this world to the abode of the Hereafter, to their lesser migration from land to land, and informed them that their return is to Him, so there is no settled dwelling for them in this abode apart from meeting Him. Then He explained to them the condition of those who are patient in the trial for Him: that He will settle them in gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. So He consoled them for the land and home they left for His sake, which had been their dwelling, by settling them in a home better than it, more gathering of every good, pleasure and bliss, with eternal immortality, and that this is by their patience in the trial and their trust in their Lord. Then He informed them that He guarantees their provision in other than their land, just as He provided for them in their land. So they should not worry about carrying their provision: how many a creature travels from place to place without carrying its provision. Then He informed them that the period of trial and testing in this abode is very short compared with the abode of life and permanence. Then the Exalted mentioned the end of the people of trial who did not believe in Him, that their stay in this abode is enjoyment, and that they will know, at their removal from it, what they missed of the lasting bliss and what they gained of painful punishment. And He mentioned the end of the people of trial who believed in Him, obeyed His messengers, and strove against their selves and their enemy in the abode of trial, what He guides and helps them to. So the Exalted informed that the greatest of His gifts and its most excellent, in this world and the Hereafter, belongs to the people of trial who were patient under His trial and trusted in Him, and He informed that the greatest and most grievous of His punishment belongs to those who were not patient under His trial, fled from it, and preferred immediate comfort over it.

So the content of this surah is the secret of creation and command, for it is the surah of trial and testing, and the explanation of the condition of the people of affliction in this world and the Hereafter. Whoever reflects on its opening, its middle and its end will find within it that the beginning of the matter is trial and testing, its middle is patience and trust, and its end is guidance and victory. And God is the One sought for help, which clarifies it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verse 5:

In the Musnad of the Imam Ahmad, on the authority of Ammar ibn Yasir: "He prayed a prayer and made it brief, and he was asked about that, so he said: Indeed, I supplicated in it with the supplications that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate with: O Allah, I ask You by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, grant me life when life is good for me, and cause me to die when death is good for me. O Allah, I ask You for Your fear in the unseen and the witnessed, and I ask You for the word of truth in anger and in contentment, and I ask You for moderation in poverty and in wealth, and I ask You for a bounty that does not end, and I ask You for a coolness of the eye that does not cease, and I ask You for the coolness of life after death, and I ask You for the delight of looking upon Your Face, and I ask You for longing for meeting You, without a harmful adversity that harms or a misguiding trial that misleads. O Allah, adorn us with the adornment of faith, and make us guides who are guided."

And in another report: "The longing of the righteous for meeting Me has grown long, and I am more longing for meeting them."

This is the meaning that he (ﷺ) expressed with his saying: "Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him."

And some of the people of insight said concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting of Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 5].

When He, glorified be He, knew the intensity of the longing of His friends for His meeting, and that their hearts would not be guided without meeting Him, He set for them a term and an appointment for that meeting, and their souls would be at rest with it. The most pleasant and sweetest of lives, absolutely, is the life of the lovers, the longing ones, the intimate ones. Their life is the true good life, and there is no life for the heart more pleasant, more blessed, or more serene than it, and it is the good life in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97].

(Section)

Whoever complains of longing from the length of separation,
endure, perhaps tomorrow you will meet the one you love.

Journey to Him with the fire of longing, striving,
perhaps you will find guidance in the fire of passion.

The sincere lover, whenever he draws near to his beloved, his longing increases.

The greatest longing is on a day
when the tents draw near to the tents.

Whenever the lover's gaze falls upon his beloved, its seeing renews longing upon his longing.

His glance does not turn from him when it sees him
until it returns to him longing.

The sincere lover, when his gaze travels through existence, finds no path for it except to his beloved.

So when his sight turns away from him, it returns to him, dazed and exhausted.

And my glance roams among the people and turns back,
and the pupil of my eye is drowned in tears,

so it returns rejected to You, and it has
no path to anything except to You.

The most pleasant thing to the eyes of the lover is his seclusion with his beloved in secret.

My teacher's acquaintance related: that in the early stage of his affair he went out to the desert in the morning, and when he reached open land he breathed a long sigh, then recited the verse of the poet:

And I go out from among the houses, perhaps
I may, by your absence, make the heart free and alone with the secret.

[Chapter: The Station of Longing]

Among the stations of "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" is the station of longing.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting of Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 5].

It has been said: this is a consolation for the longing ones and a comfort for them. That is, I know that whoever hopes for My meeting is longing for Me, so I have set for him a term that will be soon, for it is surely coming, and everything that is coming is near.

In it there is another subtle point, which is the consoling of the longing ones with the hope of meeting.

Were it not for seeking relief through hope, the soul of the lover would be cut off from ardent love and longing,

and his heart would almost melt from what he suffers of regret and burning.

Until, when the breath of hope reaches him, the blaze subsides when he is consoled with the meeting.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his supplication:
"I ask You for the delight of looking upon Your Face, and for longing for Your meeting."

Some of them said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was constantly in longing for the meeting of Allah. His longing for His meeting never ceased. But longing has a hundred parts: ninety-nine of them belong to Him, and one part is distributed among the Ummah.

So he (ﷺ) wished that this part be added to the longing that is specific to him. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

[Chapter: Longing Is One of the Effects of Love]

Longing is one of the effects of love and one of its rulings, for it is the journey of the heart toward the beloved in every state.

It has been said: it is the agitation of hearts toward the meeting with the beloved.

It has been said: it is the burning of the inner organs; from it it is aroused and generated, it sets hearts ablaze and cuts livers apart.

And love is higher than it, because longing is generated from it, and it grows strong or weak according to its measure.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: The sign of longing is the weaning of the limbs from desires.

Abu 'Uthman said: Its sign is loving death together with ease and well-being, like the state of Yusuf: when he was thrown into the well he did not say "cause me to die," and when he was entered into prison he did not say "cause me to die," but when the matter, the security and the blessing were complete for him, he said: "Cause me to die as a Muslim."

Ibn Khafif said: Longing is the stirring of hearts with ecstasy, and love of meeting through nearness.

It has been said: it is a flame that arises within the innermost parts of the chest, arising from separation; when meeting occurs it is extinguished.

I say: this is a matter of dispute among the lovers, namely: does longing cease with meeting or not?

And they do not differ that love does not cease with meeting.

Some of them said: it ceases with meeting, because longing is the journey of the heart toward its beloved. When it arrives at him and reaches him, the place of longing becomes the coolness of the eye through him. This coolness combines with love and does not contradict it.

They said: when the predominant state of the heart is witnessing the beloved, longing does not visit it.

It was said to one of them: Do you long for Him? He said: No. Longing is only for an absent one, and He is present.

And a group said: rather, longing increases with nearness and arrival, and does not cease. For before arrival it was based on report and knowledge, and after it, it has become on direct vision and witnessing. For this reason it was said:

And longing is most intense on a day
when the tents draw near to the tents.

Al-Junayd said: I heard al-Sarri say: Longing is the most sublime station of the knower when it is realized in him. And when it is realized in longing, it removes him from everything that preoccupies him from the one he longs for. On this basis, the people of Paradise are always in longing for Allah, despite their nearness to Him and their seeing Him.

They said: Among the proofs that longing is greater during the state of meeting is that we see the lover weeping at the meeting with his beloved. That weeping is only from the intensity of his longing for him and his ecstasy with him, and therefore he finds at his meeting a kind of longing that he did not find in the state of his absence from him.

[Chapter: Degrees of Longing]

[The First Degree: The Longing of the Worshipper for Paradise]

He said: It is of three degrees. The first degree: the longing of the worshipper for Paradise, so that the fearful may be secure, the grieving may rejoice, and the hopeful may triumph.

That is, the longing of the worshipper for Paradise contains these three wisdoms.

The first of them: the attainment of security, which arouses hope. For fear that is stripped of security from every aspect does not move its bearer to any action at all unless hope accompanies it. If it is stripped of hope, it is cut off and becomes despair.

The second: the joy of the grieving. For grief stripped of joy, too, if joy does not accompany it, kills its bearer. Were it not for the spirit of joy, the grieving one's faculties would be disabled and his grief would sit him down; but when grief sits him down, the spirit of joy rises in him.

The third: the spirit of triumph. For if the hopeful is not accompanied by the spirit of triumph, his hope dies. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Second Degree: Longing for Allah, Mighty and Majestic]

He said: The second degree: longing for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which love planted, the love that grows on the edges of bounties, so his heart clings to His holy attributes and he longs to witness the subtleties of His generosity, the signs of His righteousness, and the markers of His grace. This is a longing that is covered by pleasures, that is mixed with joys, and that is resisted by patience.

Longing for Allah does not contradict longing for Paradise. For the best of what is in Paradise is His nearness, seeing Him, hearing His speech, and His pleasure. Yes. Longing for mere eating, drinking, and the wide-eyed houris in Paradise is very deficient compared with the longing of the lovers for Allah, the Exalted; indeed, there is absolutely no comparison to it. And this longing has two degrees.

One of them: a longing planted by love whose cause is kindness and favor. This is what he referred to when he said: it grows on the edges of bounties. Its cause is contemplating Allah's favor, kindness, and blessings.

This has already been explained in the station of love, and it became clear that love of the Names and Attributes is more perfect and stronger than love of kindness and gifts.

His saying "grows on the edges of bounties," meaning its sides, indicates that it has not become firmly established and strong, and that it is from the growth of the edges, which are the sides of bounties, not from the growth of the Names and Attributes.

His saying "so his heart clings to His holy attributes" means the attributes specific to bounty and kindness, such as the Righteous, the Bestower, the Benevolent, the Generous, the Giver, the Forgiving, and similar.

His saying "holy" means pure, exalted above the interpretation of distorters, the likening of those who liken, and the negation of those who negate.

We said that what he intends is these specific attributes for two reasons.

The first: the attachment of the heart to general attributes occurs only in the third degree.

The second: he made the fruit of this attachment the servant's longing to witness the subtleties of the Lord's generosity, bounties, and kindness, and the signs of His righteousness. These are the marks of His righteousness toward the servant and His kindness to him; likewise "the markers of His grace," which is what He bestows upon him and by which He prefers him over others.

His saying "This is a longing that is covered by pleasures" means: it is a longing that is caused, not purely for the essence of the beloved, but for what one attains from Him of pleasures. "Covered" means that pleasures have overtaken it.

His saying "and it is mixed with joys" means: it is pulled. For mixing (al-mukhalaja) is pulling. When joy mingles with this longing, it is mixed with a kind of personal share.

His saying "and it is resisted by patience" means: its bearer is strong in endurance, so his patience resists his longing and does not overcome it, unlike the longing of the third degree.

[Section: The Third Degree: Pure Longing]

He said: The third degree: a fire kindled by the purity of love, which has embittered life, stripped away consolation, and was not calmed by any station short of meeting.

He means: longing in this level is like the fire kindled by the purity of love, which is its pure essence. He likened it to fire because of its burning in the innermost parts.

His saying "the purity of love" indicates that it is a love not for the sake of gifts and blessings, but a love attached to the Essence and the Attributes.

His saying "which has embittered life" means it prevents its bearer from settling into pleasant living. "Embittering" is close to troubling.

His saying "and stripped away consolation" means it plundered consolation and took it by force.

"Consolation" (al-salwa) is deliverance from the distress of love, and laying down its burden from the back, and turning away from the beloved in forgetfulness.

His saying "was not calmed by any station short of meeting" means: no resting place short of meeting the beloved would suffice for it or turn it back. This is what endurance cannot resist, for no resting place short of meeting the one he loves can calm it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verse 25:

And Abraham, His intimate friend, said to his people: ﴿You have only taken idols besides Allah as a bond of affection among yourselves in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.﴾

This is the condition of everyone who shares in an aim: they show affection for one another as long as they are helping each other to attain it. When that aim is cut off, it leaves behind regret, sorrow and pain, and that affection turns into hatred, cursing, and blame of one another, because the aim has turned into sorrow and punishment. This is observed in this world in the state of those who share in its disgrace when they are seized and punished. Thus, every two people who help each other in falsehood and feel affection for each other on its account will inevitably see their affection turn into hatred and enmity.

The beneficial principle regarding mixing with people (al-khulṭah) is that one mixes with people in good matters, such as the Friday prayer and congregational prayer, the festivals and the Hajj, the seeking of knowledge, jihad, and giving sincere counsel, and that one withdraws from them in evil matters and in the excess of permissible things. If there is a need to mix with them in evil and one cannot withdraw from them, then one must be extremely cautious not to agree with them, and must be patient with their harm, for they will inevitably harm him if he has no strength and no helper.

However, harm that is followed by honour, love for him, esteem, and praise of him from them, from the believers, and from the Lord of the worlds, is better. Agreeing with them, on the other hand, is followed by humiliation, hatred of him, abhorrence, and blame from them, from the believers, and from the Lord of the worlds.

Therefore, patience over their harm is better, with a better outcome and a more praiseworthy end. If there is a need to mix with them in the excess of permissible things, then he should strive to turn that gathering into an act of obedience to Allah if he is able, encourage himself, strengthen his heart, and not pay attention to the satanic whisper that cuts him off from this, claiming that this is showing off and love for displaying his knowledge and his state, and the like. Rather, he should fight that whisper, seek help from Allah, and influence them with whatever good he can.

If the decrees of fate prevent him from doing that, then let him withdraw his heart from among them as a hair is drawn out of dough, and let him be present among them while absent, near while far, asleep while awake: he looks at them but does not see them, and hears their speech but does not comprehend it, because he has taken his heart from among them and raised it to the Highest Assembly, swimming around the Throne with the pure, exalted spirits. How difficult and burdensome this is for souls! Yet it is easy for the one whom Allah makes it easy for. Between the servant and this state is that he be truthful with Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, persist in turning to Him, and cast himself at His door, prostrate and humbled. Nothing helps in this except a true love, constant remembrance of Allah with the heart and tongue, and avoidance of the four remaining corrupting things that will be mentioned later. This is not attained except with righteous preparation, a source of strength from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, a sincere resolve, and freedom from attachment to anything other than Allah, the Exalted. And Allah knows best.

"He was asked (ﷺ) about the words of the Exalted, ﴿And you commit in your gatherings the evil [deed]﴾

He said: They used to pelt the passersby with pebbles (yakhdhifun) and mock them, and that was the evil deed they used to commit."

Mentioned by Ahmad.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verse 41:

He, glory be to Him, mentioned that they are weak, and that those who took them as their protectors (awliya') are weaker than them. So they, in their weakness and in what they intended by taking protectors, are like the spider that has taken a house, and it is the weakest and feeblest of houses. Under this parable is the point that these polytheists are at their weakest when they take, besides Allah, protectors, and they gain nothing from those whom they take as protectors except weakness, as the Exalted said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be for them a source of might. No! They will reject their worship of them and will be against them opponents﴾ [Maryam: 81-82].

And the Exalted said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be helped. They are unable to help them, while they are an army brought forward for them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74-75].

And He said, after mentioning the destruction of the polytheist nations: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. And their gods, which they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them at all when the command of your Lord came, and they increased them in nothing but ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

So these are four places in the Qur'an which indicate that whoever takes a protector besides Allah, seeking strength through him, pride through him, and victory through him, obtains from him nothing but the opposite of his aim. The Qur'an contains more than this, and this is among the finest of parables and the most indicative of the falsehood of shirk, the loss of its adherent, and his obtaining the opposite of his aim.

If it is said: They know that the weakest of houses is the spider's house, so how did He negate their knowledge of that by His saying: ﴿if only they knew﴾?

The answer: He, glory be to Him, did not negate from them their knowledge of the weakness of the spider's house. Rather, He negated from them their knowledge that taking protectors besides Him is like the spider that has taken a house. Had they known that, they would not have done it. But they thought that taking protectors besides Him would bring them might and power, so the matter was contrary to what they supposed.

(Benefit)

From the coining of parables in the Qur'an, there are benefits: admonition, exhortation, encouragement, deterrence, taking lesson, affirmation, bringing the intended meaning close to the intellect, and depicting it in the form of the perceptible, such that its relation to the intellect is like the relation of the perceptible to the senses.

Parables of the Qur'an may also include an explanation of the difference in reward according to praise and blame, and of reward and punishment, and of magnifying or belittling a matter, and of establishing one matter and nullifying another. And Allah knows best.

(Subtlety)

Among the wondrous tricks of the spider is that it weaves that web as a snare for prey, then lies in wait inside it. When gnats and flies become caught in it, it pounces on them and sucks their blood. This depicts the hunting by snare and net, whereas the former depicts the hunting of dogs and leopards. Do not disdain the lesson from a trivial thing, such as an ant or a mosquito, for a precious meaning may be drawn from a trivial thing. Disdaining this is an inheritance from those whose intellects rejected that Allah, Exalted, struck in His Book parables with the fly, the spider, the dog and the donkey. So Allah sent down: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not shy to strike an example — of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾.

How abundant and numerous are the wisdoms in these animals that you disdain and belittle! How many indications of the Creator, His subtlety, His mercy and His wisdom are in them! Ask the one who denies (divine attributes) who inspired them with these tricks and this gentleness in hunting their prey, which is their sustenance, and who gave these tricks to them in place of what He took from them of strength and power. He made sufficient for them what He gave them of cunning in place of what He took from them of strength and power. None but the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verse 45:

It has been said: the meaning is that you remember God during prayer, and He remembers you, and God's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Salman, Abu al-Darda and Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with them.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from ʿAṭiyya, regarding "and the remembrance of God is greater": he said, it is His saying, ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾.

So God's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him.

Ibn Zayd and Qatada said: its meaning is, and the remembrance of God is greater than everything.

Salman was asked: Which deeds are the best? He said: Do you not recite the Qur'an, "and the remembrance of God is greater"?

What supports this is the hadith (saying of the Prophet ﷺ) of Abu al-Darda: "Shall I not tell you of the best of your deeds, the purest of them in the sight of your King, and better for you than spending gold and silver? …" (the hadith continues).

Shaykh al-Islam Abu al-ʿAbbas Ibn Taymiyya, may God sanctify his soul, used to say:

The correct view is that the meaning of the verse is that prayer has two great purposes, one of which is greater than the other.

For it forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and it includes the remembrance of God; and the remembrance of God that is in it is greater than its forbidding of indecency and wrongdoing.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was asked which deed is best. He said: the remembrance of God is greater.

(Section)

7. As for the report that His remembrance is greater than everything, it is like His saying, ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of God is greatest﴾.

On it there are four views:

The first: that the remembrance of God is greater than everything, and therefore it is the best of acts of worship, because the purpose of all acts of worship is the establishment of His remembrance; so it is the essence (sirr) of acts of worship and their spirit.

The second: that the meaning is: when you remember Him, He remembers you, so His remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him.

According to this, the verbal noun (maṣdar) is an annexation to the agent (subject); according to the first, it is an annexation to the object remembered.

The third: that the meaning is: the remembrance of God is too great for indecency and wrongdoing to remain with it; rather, when the remembrance is complete, it erases every sin and disobedience. This is what the exegetes (mufassirūn) have mentioned.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may God have mercy on him, say: the meaning of the verse is that prayer has two great benefits.

The first: its forbidding of indecency and wrongdoing.

The second: its containing the remembrance of God, and its embodying it. And the remembrance of God that it embodies is greater than its forbidding of indecency and wrongdoing.

(Section)

The tenth stage of the stages of life:

It is the everlasting, enduring life that comes after this world is folded up and the worldly life and its people perish, in the abode of life (dar al-hayawan). It is the life toward which the diligent strive, which the racers race toward, and which the competitors compete for. It is the life to which we have directed our discourse, and to which all the heavenly Books and the messengers of God have called. It is the life of which one who has failed to prepare for it says: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, and your Lord comes with the angels, rank upon rank, and Hell is brought forth that day—on that day man will remember, but how will the remembrance benefit him? He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life." So on that day none will punish as He punishes, and none will bind as He binds﴾ [al-Fajr 89:21–26]. It is the life of which God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. And indeed, the Last Abode—that is the life, if they only knew﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 29:64].

The life that precedes it is like sleep in comparison to it. Everything that preceded of the description of the journey (sayr), its stations, the states of the travelers, and their outward and inward servitude is a means to this life. The worldly life is only in comparison to it, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The world in comparison to the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him look at what it returns with."

And as it has been said: The Hereafter breathed, and the world became one of its breaths. So the people of happiness experience the breath of its bliss, and they act upon that breath; and the people of misery experience the breath of its punishment, and they act upon that breath.

If the life of the people of faith and righteous deeds in this abode is a good life, then what is the assumption about their life in the barzakh (intermediate realm), since they have been freed from the prison and constriction of the world? What then is the assumption about their life in the abode of lasting bliss that does not pass away, where they see the face of their Lord, blessed and exalted, morning and evening, and hear His address?

If you say: What is the cause of the soul's failure to seek this life, which has no equal, and what made it indifferent to it? And what is the cause of its desire for the transient, perishing life, which is like a dream and a sleep? Is it corruption in its perception and feeling? Or denial of that life? Or a defect in the intellect and blindness there? Or preference for the present, seen with the eyes, over the absent, known through faith?

It is said: Rather, it is due to a combination of all these matters.

The strongest of the causes in this is weakness of faith, for faith is the spirit of deeds; it is what moves one to them, commands the best of them, and forbids the worst of them. In proportion to the strength of faith is the force of its command and prohibition to its possessor, and the possessor's compliance and restraint. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: How wretched is what your faith commands you, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqara 2:93].

In summary: when faith is strong, the longing for this life grows strong, and its possessor's pursuit of it intensifies.

The second cause: the heaviness of heedlessness upon the heart. For heedlessness is the sleep of the heart. Thus you find many who are awake in the senses but asleep in reality; you think them awake while they are asleep. This is the opposite of one who is alert in heart while his body sleeps. For when life is strong in the heart, it does not sleep when the body sleeps. The perfection of this life belonged to our Prophet ﷺ and to whomever God has given life to his heart through love of Him and following His message, with insight into that, according to his share of both.

Heedlessness and wakefulness occur in the senses, the intellect and the heart. So the heart that is alert or heedless is like the body that is awake or asleep. Just as wakefulness of the senses has two kinds, so too wakefulness of the heart has two kinds.

The first kind of wakefulness of the senses is that its possessor penetrates sensory matters and delves into them by his effort and shrewdness, his cunning and his skill in managing them.

The second kind is that he turns toward his self, his heart and his essence, and cares about achieving its perfection. He observes the lofty and the base matters, prefers the higher over the lower, gives precedence to the better of two goods by forfeiting the lesser of them, commits the lesser of two evils to avoid the greater of them, and adorns himself with noble character and lofty qualities, so that his outward appearance is beautiful, his inward being is more beautiful than his outward, and his secret is better than his public. He competes with the people of lofty qualities for them as people compete for gold and silver. Through this wakefulness he prepares himself for the other two kinds.

One of these two is a wakefulness that moves him to acquire the everlasting, enduring life, which has no equal, from this transient, perishing life, which has no value.

If you say: Illustrate for me how the everlasting life is acquired from the perishing life, and how this happens, for I do not understand it.

I say: This too is from the sleep of the heart, indeed from its death. Is the everlasting life acquired except from this passing life? You may light your lamp from another lamp that has nearly gone out; the second catches fire and shines to the utmost brightness, its light joins with it, and the first goes out. The one who acquires his everlasting life from his cut-off life only moves from a cut-off abode to an enduring abode, and death has intervened between the two abodes. It is a bridge that none crosses to that abode except by it, and a door through which none enters it except through it. Thus there are two lives in two abodes with death between them. Just as the light of that abode is acquired from the light of this abode, so its life is likewise acquired from its life. In proportion to the light of faith in this abode is the servant's light in that abode, and in proportion to his life in this abode is his life there.

Yes: this light and life from which that light and life is acquired does not cease; rather, it shines for the servant in the barzakh, at the standing of the Resurrection, and upon the Path (sirat). It does not leave him until the abode of life. The sun's light is extinguished, but this light is not extinguished; sensory life is annulled, but this life is not annulled. This is one of the two kinds of wakefulness of the heart.

The second kind: a wakefulness that leads to a life which expression cannot reach, imagination cannot attain, and words never exactly match its meaning. What is pointed to by it is the life of the lover with his beloved, on whom the stability of his heart, spirit and life depends, who is indispensable to him, not even for the blink of an eye, and in whom lies the coolness of his eye, the tranquility of his heart and the rest of his spirit. He needs Him more than his hearing, his sight and his strength, and even more than his life, for his life without Him is torment, pains, worries and sorrows. His life is contingent upon nearness to Him, love for Him and companionship with Him. The torment of being veiled from Him is greater than the other torment. Just as the bliss of the heart and spirit by removing that veil is greater than the bliss of eating, drinking, and enjoying the maidens with lustrous eyes, so the torment of the veil is greater than the torment of the Blazing Fire. For this reason God, glorified is He, combined for His friends the two blisses in His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna) and an increase (ziyada)﴾ [Yunus 10:26]. The best is Paradise, and the increase is the vision of His noble Face in the Gardens of Eden. And He combined for His enemies the two torments in His saying: ﴿No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day. Then indeed, they will be burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 83:15–16].

The point is: heedlessness is the sleep of the heart from seeking this life, and it is a veil upon it. If this veil is not uncovered by remembrance, it thickens until it becomes a veil of idleness, play and preoccupation with what does not benefit. If he hastens to uncover it, well and good; otherwise it thickens until it becomes a veil of disobedience and minor sins that distance him from God. If he hastens to uncover it, well and good; otherwise it thickens until it becomes a veil of major sins that bring upon him the Lord's wrath, anger and curse. If he hastens to uncover it, well and good; otherwise it thickens until it becomes a veil of practical innovations (bida ʿamaliyya), through which the doer torments himself and which benefit him nothing. If he hastens to uncover it, well and good; otherwise it thickens until it becomes a veil of verbal, doctrinal innovations, which contain lying about God and His Messenger and denial of the truth the Messenger brought. If he hastens to uncover it, well and good; otherwise it thickens until it becomes a veil of doubt and denial, which undermines the five foundations of faith: belief in God, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the meeting with Him. Because of the thickness, density, darkness and blackness of this veil, he does not see the realities of faith, and Satan takes hold of him, promising and deceiving him, while the commanding self (nafs ammara bi-l-su') desires and craves. The authority of nature has overcome the authority of faith, captured and imprisoned it if it has not destroyed it. It takes charge of the kingdom, employs the armies of desires, and assigns to them the habits upon which the work proceeds. It shuts the door of wakefulness and posts over it the gatekeeper of heedlessness, saying: "Beware lest we be approached from your side." It appoints a chamberlain from among caprice, saying: "Beware lest you allow anyone to enter upon me except with you. The affair of this kingdom has come to you and to the gatekeeper. O gatekeeper of heedlessness, and O chamberlain of caprice, let each of you keep his post. If you leave it empty, the affairs of our kingdom will be corrupted, the rule will return to others, and the authority of faith will make us taste the worst of disgrace and humiliation, and we will never rejoice in this city again."

There is no god but God! When these armies gather upon the heart, along with the weakness of faith, the scarcity of helpers, turning away from the remembrance of the Merciful, joining the ranks of the sons of the age, long hope which corrupts the human being, and his preferring the hastened, present life over the absent one promised after these worlds are folded up, then God is the one sought for help, and upon Him is reliance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verses 51–52:

In the Marasil of Abu Dawud it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in the hand of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab a leaf containing something of the Torah, and said:

"Enough is it for a people to be misguided that they follow a book other than their own book, which was revealed to a prophet other than their prophet."

So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾

And the Exalted said, to those who asked for a sign that would attest to the truthfulness of His Messenger: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe. (51) Say: Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. And those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah, those are the losers. (52)﴾

He, glory be to Him, informed that the Book which He sent down to His Messenger suffices in place of every sign. In it is the proof and the indication that it is from Allah, and that Allah, glory be to Him, sent His Messenger with it, and in it is the clarification of what brings happiness to whoever follows it and saves him from punishment.

Then He said: ﴿Say: Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth.﴾

Since Allah, glory be to Him, knows all things, His testimony is the most truthful and the most just testimony, for it is a testimony based on perfect knowledge, encompassing what is testified to. Thus the one who bears witness by it is the most just and truthful of witnesses. He, glory be to Him, mentions His knowledge when He bears witness, His power and dominion when He recompenses, His wisdom when He creates and commands, His mercy when He mentions the sending of His Messenger, His forbearance when He mentions the sins and disobedience of His servants, His hearing when He mentions their supplication, and His might and knowledge when He decrees and ordains.

So reflect upon the occurrence of His Most Beautiful Names in His Book, and their connection with creation and command, and with reward and punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 29, verse 64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter — that is the (true) Life﴾

What is meant is Paradise, according to the people of tafsir (exegesis).

They said: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter﴾ means Paradise, ﴿that is the Life﴾ means it is the abode of life in which there is no death.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a life in which there is no death.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is the abode of everlasting life.

The people of language (ahl al-lughah) agree that al-hayawan (ḥayawān, "life", "living existence") means al-hayah (ḥayāh, "life").

Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said: al-hayah and al-hayawan are the same.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-ḥayāh, al-ḥayawān, and al-ḥayy (with a kasra on the ḥā') are one and the same.

Abu 'Ali said: he means that they are verbal nouns (maṣādir). So ḥayāh is of the pattern fa'lah, like ḥalbah; ḥayawān is like nazawān and ghalayān; and ḥayy is like 'ayy.

Al-'Ajjaj said:

"We were there when life was (fully) alive"

meaning: when life was (truly) life.

As for Abu Zayd, he differed from them and said: al-ḥayawān is that which has a soul (rūḥ), while al-mawtān and al-mawāt are that which has no soul.

The correct view is that al-ḥayawān applies in two ways:

The first is a verbal noun, as Abu 'Ubaydah related.

The second is an adjective, as Abu Zayd related.

According to Abu Zayd's view, al-ḥayawān is like al-ḥayy, the opposite of the dead. The first view was preferred on the ground that the pattern fa'lān is primarily for verbal nouns, like nazawān and ghalayān, unlike adjectives, whose pattern is fa'lān, like sakrān and ghaḍbān.

Those who preferred the second view replied that fa'lān has also come in adjectives. They said: a man who is ḍamyān (quick and light), and zafyān (swift).

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon) it is said: a zafyān she-camel is swift, and a zafyān bow is one that releases the arrow swiftly.

Thus His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter — that is the (true) Life﴾ may bear two meanings:

The first is that the Hereafter is (true) life because there is no turbidity in it and no ending for it.

That is, nothing troubles it as troubles life in this abode, so al-hayawān is a verbal noun in this sense.

The second is that the meaning is: it is the abode that does not perish, does not cease, and is not annihilated, as the living perish in this world. It is therefore more worthy of this name than the living creature (al-hayawān) that perishes and dies.

(Fa'ida)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾

He, glorified be He, linked guidance to striving (jihad). So the people most complete in guidance are those most excellent in striving. The best jihad is the jihad of the self (jihad al-nafs), the jihad of desire (jihad al-hawa), the jihad of Satan (jihad al-shaytan), and the jihad of the world (jihad al-dunya).

Whoever strives against these four for the sake of God, God guides him to the paths of His pleasure, which lead to His Garden.

Whoever abandons striving loses guidance in proportion to the striving he has neglected.

Al-Junayd said: ﴿And those who strive﴾ against their desires, ﴿for Us﴾ through repentance, ﴿We will surely guide them﴾ to the paths of sincerity (al-ikhlas).

No one can be fully empowered to fight his enemy outwardly unless he has struggled against these enemies inwardly. Whoever is victorious over them is victorious over his enemy, and whoever is overcome by them is overcome by his enemy.

(Latifa)

Al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mubarak said: When people differ over a matter, look at what the people of the frontier (ahl al-thaghr), meaning the people of jihad, hold, for God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed God is with the good-doers﴾.

(Fasl)

Know that the reality of patience with God is the steadfastness of the heart through remaining upright with Him, and that it does not swerve from Him like the swerving of foxes here and there. The reality of this is uprightness toward Him and the heart's devotion to Him.

Some scholars added another division of it and called it "patience in Him" (al-sabr fihi).

This too does not fall outside the aforementioned divisions of patience, and no meaning of patience in Him is conceivable other than patience for His sake. This is like saying "I did this in God and for Him," as Khubayb said:

"That, in the Essence of God, and if He wills, He will bless the scattered pieces of a torn body."

And God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾

And He said: ﴿And strive in God﴾

In the hadith of Jabir: "When God, Exalted is He, brought his father back to life, He said to him, 'Ask what you wish.' He said, 'O Lord, that You return me to the world so that I may be killed in You a second time.'"

And [the Prophet] said: "I was harmed in God, and no one has been harmed like I was."

This phrase has two meanings. The first is that it is for His good pleasure, obedience and path, and this concerns what a person does by his own choice, as in the hadith: "I learned knowledge for You (fika)."

The second is that it occurred because of Him and on account of Him, and this concerns what befalls a person without his choice. Most of the uses of their saying "that is in God" fall under this meaning.

So reflect on his saying "I was harmed in God," and Khubayb's saying "that, in the Essence of God," and 'Abd Allah ibn Haram's saying "until I am killed in You."

Likewise His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, since harm follows upon it for His sake, glorified be He.

Here "fi" is not used for location, nor merely for causation, although causation is its original sense. Consider his saying "the blood-money of a believer is a hundred camels" and his saying "a woman entered the Fire because of a cat": how you find in it a meaning beyond mere causation. "Fi" is not in all its senses for containment. So your saying "I did this in Your good pleasure" carries a meaning added to "I did this for Your good pleasure." And when you say "I was harmed in God," this phrase is not replaced by "I was harmed for God" or "because of God."

Once the meaning is understood, the wording's form is set aside. The point is that patience in God, if this meaning is intended, is true; but if it is meant as something outside patience under His decrees, His commands and His prohibitions, and not for Him and by Him, then it is not achieved.

The one who is patient in God is like the one who strives in God, and striving in Him does not fall outside the meaning of striving by Him and for Him. And God is the Granter of success.
